newsitem.title: UK: EMU bond contenders lashed in latest week-Salomon.
newsitem.headline: EMU bond contenders lashed in latest week-Salomon.

text.p: European bonds took a beating this week as single currency tensions flared in its two staunchest supporters -- France and Germany, data from Salomon Brothers showed on Friday.
Markets away from the EMU fray benefited, with Australia chalking up the biggest gains after an interest rate cut.
Salomon's overall World Government Bond Index fell 0.05 in the week ended May 29 in local currency terms.
The biggest losers in Europe were France and Finland, each registering losses of 0.38 percent in local currencies, followed by Sweden which had a negative return of 0.26 percent.
Peripherals Italy and Spain lost 0.31 and 0.18 respectively.

Results from the first round of French elections on Sunday set the tone for the week after left wing parties emerged well ahead, throwing up questions about France's commitment to getting its books in order for EMU.

And in Germany, a furious row erupted about the government's plans to revalue gold reserves to help it make the EMU grade. The Bundesbank flatly rejected the plan but Bonn said it would go ahead regardless.
All this left European markets in a daze, and convergence trades upside down as German yields rose to price in a softer euro.
German bonds slipped 0.01 percent in the week in mark terms.
Meanwhile, British gilts posted gains of 0.32 percent, Switzerland a 0.40 percent gain and Denmark 0.16, in local currency terms.
Australia was tops with a 1.01 percent increase after the Reserve bank cut its cash rate to 5.50 percent from 6.00 percent last Friday.
U.S. Treasuries registered a gain of 0.15 percent while Canadian bonds trailed with a 0.15 percent loss.
Japanese government bonds declined 0.38 percent in the week in yen terms.
In U.S. dollar terms, French bonds lost 1.32 percent and Swedish bonds 1.89 percent and Italy 0.99 percent European currencies weakened amid the EMU friction.

Salomon's bond index is calculated using all government bonds with over one year to maturity, weighted for market capitalisation. Only bonds freely available to institutional investors and with a certain minimum amount outstanding are included. Returns take account of price moves and accrued interest.
